entry.what: The event loop calls one turn function per environment (made at module init, referenced from the instance), with the Host as its argument and a second naming the handle (setImmediate(turn, host, 0), setTimeout(turn, ms, host, 1)), so scheduling makes no function and a pending handle holds the Host. A delay is milliseconds rounded by double arithmetic and clamped to 2^31-1 (setTimeout fires at once beyond it); an early fire is an idle turn that arms the rest. entry.what: A service handler that returns a thenable (an async function, a plain function returning a promise) is refused: TypeError "a service handler returns the service, not a promise ...", the invocation kept as failed and the invoker given error.communication, the error reported after the turn. The promise is not awaited and its later rejection stays unhandled.
entry.why: The plan asked to decide whether to await it. Python's handlers are synchronous. Awaiting would leave the service missing while sends to it arrive: they would be dropped or need a queue the addon does not have (no tables of its own). The Invocation is a record that outlives the ack, so a plain handler can return the service at once and answer later. Refusing shows the mistake at once and loses no message without a trace.
entry.evidence: tinyactors-napi/src/effects.c ta_napi_dispatch_invoke; test/services.test.mjs: 'a handler that returns a promise is refused: the service is what it returns'
entry.resolution: Revised (the maintainer, 2026-10-17: in Node every continuation runs on the same thread's event loop, so preserve core's invariants while meeting what a JavaScript programmer expects): a service handler may return a promise of the service. The entry is "starting" until it settles; sends to it (IO_PROCESSOR TA_NIL) and an UNINVOKE that come meanwhile are made records before their ack (as a promise-returning I/O processor's send is) and given to receive/stop in order once it resolves; a rejection is a failed start (error.communication to the invoker and to each queued send with its sendid), reported as the loop reports errors; an UNINVOKE before it settles stops the service as soon as it resolves. Nothing runs inside a run; nothing outlives an ack as a view. Implemented in p2-decisions.

entry.what: A receive that returns a thenable has its Send view filled before the ack, as an I/O processor's view is (d-async). Its rejection is a crash: if the invocation has not ended, the invoker gets error.communication with the send's sendid and the entry stays failed without the service (dropped, not stopped). The rejection goes on, unhandled. This uses a function bound to the invocation and the view (instance->crashed). stop() is called; what it returns is not followed.
entry.why: Python has no async receive. In JavaScript an async receive (await fetch, then sendBack) is the common shape, and it must read send.data after an await. A rejection is the async form of a receive that throws, which Python treats as a crash.
entry.evidence: src/effects.c ta_napi_dispatch_service_send, ta_napi_service_crashed; test/services.test.mjs: 'an async receive reads its send after the ack; its rejection is a crash'

entry.what: host.wake of a hibernated actor that has an event waiting is O(wake queue): ta_actor_wake unlinks it from the singly linked wake_queue by walking from the head (tinyactors-core/src/system/hibernate.c:767-778). With N/100 hibernated actors each sent an event before the run (20,000 at 2M, 40,000 at 4M), waking the last 32 of them costs 1107 us a call at 2,000,000 actors and 2949 us at 4,000,000 (ratio 2.66), against 8 us for a wake with nothing queued.

entry.what: The gate's shape, which the plan left open: two scenarios per size, each size a process of its own. 'hibernated': N counters, 1000 resident, the rest in SQLite, plus N/100 invokers with running services (so core's requests grow with N) and a named probe at the end of the table; every operation runs here. 'resident': N counters all resident in a segment left to grow from core's defaults (spawn pays its relocations, ta_system_relocate amortized); the operations whose cost may depend on the resident population (send, terminate, terminate of runnable actors, actorByName, a full actor.list, sweep, hibernate, wake, snapshot, restore, close, migrating a chart). A chart's migration of every actor runs in the resident scenario only: with wake:true over millions of hibernated actors it would wake each from the store (the migration gate's 150 s at 2M); one-session migration runs in the hibernated one. Cost: median of 5 samples of at least --min-ms (200 full, 25 fast), each sample made of batches whose setup and cleanup are untimed; an operation over the factor is measured again (both sizes) up to --attempts times and keeps its best ratio; KNOWN operations (requests to core) are reported, not failed, and not retried.
entry.why: Timer noise does not repeat across processes, a scan does; per-call costs are averaged over thousands of calls. Known core gaps must not fail mise run test, but the factor is not loosened and the README records them as failing.

entry.what: Awkward shape: await host.idle() resolves before a service answers from a promise, even one that settles in microtasks with no I/O at all. I placed an order whose payment service answers from gateway.charge(...).then(...) (an async function that awaits nothing slow) and awaited host.idle() once, expecting the order paid, shipped and delivered on a SimulatedClock; the outbox was empty. Each answer (invocation.done, sendBack) schedules a new turn after the idle one resolved, so a test needs its own loop of setImmediate and idle() (settle() in examples/order-fulfillment/test.mjs, four rounds) and a guess at how many rounds are enough. The guides say idle() waits for the host, not your promises (services.md, io-processors.md, testing.md's until() polls on the real clock), but nothing waits for both, and on a SimulatedClock there is nothing to poll on. Workaround: settle() in the example's test.
entry.evidence: examples/order-fulfillment/test.mjs, settle(); a first run with one idle() printed [] for the outbox (node 22.23.3, bun 1.4.1); docs/guide/services.md: 'await host.idle() waits for the host, not for your promises'
entry.resolution: Fixed in napi: idle() resolves only at an idle turn with no promise a handler returned pending. Every handler's result (I/O processors, the transport, a service handler and its receive, wake, telemetry, log, migrated, migrationDone, a typed method's onResult and onError) that is a thenable is followed with then (the last promise of the addon's own chain, so a rejection stays one unhandled rejection) and counted on the host (host->promises); when the count reaches zero with an idle() waiting, a turn is scheduled, which settles it. The last take's promises at close are asyncDispose's and not counted. A promise a handler starts and does not return is not waited for, and one that never settles keeps idle() pending (index.d.ts says so). Tests: test/loop.test.mjs 'idle() waits for the promises handlers return: a log handler's, a typed method's, a service's'; test/effects.test.mjs 'a handler returning a promise: its view is filled before the ack and answers after it; idle() waits for it'. Tests that looked at a service while its start promise was held (test/services.test.mjs) and examples that held an upstream or a worker while awaiting idle() (http-gateway, job-scheduler) now let turns run with setImmediate instead. Commits: 827b4d29.

entry.what: Confusing error and docs gap: an async I/O processor's send.answer() (and send.fail()) throws TA_ERROR_STALE with the message 'no live session takes this data' when the sender ended while the handler awaited (a session logged out or expired while its request was at the upstream). I expected either a no-op or an error that says the sending session has ended: io-processors.md, 'Answering later', says answer() and fail() 'work whenever the promise gets there, as long as the host is open', and index.d.ts's Send says the view stays valid 'answer and fail included, while the host is open'; neither mentions the sender's end, and the message speaks of 'data', which the handler did not pass to fail(). Uncaught, it is an unhandled rejection that fails a node:test case. Nothing tells the handler whether the sender still lives before it answers. After close() the same call throws TA_ERROR_STATE 'the Host is closed', which the docs do say. Workaround: a try/catch around answer()/fail() that swallows TA_ERROR_STALE and TA_ERROR_STATE (examples/http-gateway/gateway.mjs, urn:gateway:upstream).
entry.evidence: examples/http-gateway/test.mjs, 'a logout answers the requests behind it and in flight with 401', without the try/catch: TinyactorsError: no live session takes this data, status 'TA_ERROR_STALE', at gateway.mjs:84 (node 22, bun 1.4.1); src/host.c:923
entry.resolution: Fixed in napi: send.answer() and send.fail() return true when delivered and false when the sender ended meanwhile (ta_host_locate refuses the session, or ta_host_send gives TA_ERROR_STALE), delivering nothing; any other refusal still throws (a closed host TA_ERROR_STATE, an answer after another). Test: test/effects.test.mjs 'answer() and fail() give true when delivered and false when the sender ended; a closed host still throws'. examples/http-gateway checks host.closed and drops its try/catch. Commits: eec95150. The Python binding still raises TA_ERROR_STALE there; one rule for both is left for the maintainer: l-p4-surprises-answer-cpython.

entry.what: Docs gap: host.nextDeadline counts the telemetry encoder's flush deadline. With telemetry: { flushInterval: 1000 } and ticksPerSecond 1000, a host whose only actor had ended (its delayed sends gone) read nextDeadline 1000 instead of undefined, so a test asserting 'no timer is left' failed until the clock passed the flush. index.d.ts says 'the next deadline (a delayed send, a timeout)', and the telemetry guide does not say the flush interval is a deadline of the host's. It is reasonable (the flush must happen), but it is not what the docs describe. Workaround: the test steps the clock past the flush before asserting (examples/http-gateway/test.mjs, the idle case).
entry.evidence: examples/http-gateway/test.mjs, 'an idle session expires': actual 1000, expected undefined; a spike without telemetry gave undefined once the actor ended; index.d.ts:933-935
entry.resolution: Documented: docs/guide/telemetry.md, after the encoder's options, says a pending flush is one of the host's deadlines (nextDeadline reads it, the timer is armed for it), with a tested example on a SimulatedClock (nextDeadline 1000 after the only actor ended, undefined once flushed); index.d.ts's nextDeadline names the flush. Commits: 7a4b50a3.

entry.what: Docs gap: events already in an actor's queue when it reaches a <final> state are dropped without a trace. host.send of a request right after a logout to the same session succeeded (the actor was alive), the logout's transition ended the actor, and the request was never answered: no error.communication, no effect, nothing the application sees. That is SCXML's semantics, but the README says only that an ended actor's session 'is refused from then on', so an application that keeps a promise per event it sent (a pending HTTP response) learns of the loss only if the chart tells it. Workaround: the chart's <final> sends 'closed' to urn:gateway:http, and the gateway answers every request it still holds for that session with 401 (examples/http-gateway/gateway.mjs, sessionClosed).
entry.evidence: spike, node 22: host.send(s, 'logout'); host.send(s, 'req') on a chart whose 'req' sends to urn:x and whose 'logout' targets a <final>: both sends returned, the urn:x handler was never called, nothing was thrown; README.md, 'Actors, sessions and addresses'
entry.resolution: Documented: the README ("Actors, sessions and addresses") says the events still queued when an actor ends are dropped, as SCXML ends the session, and docs/guide/io-processors.md, "When the sender ends", shows the pattern of telling the application first: the <final>'s onentry sends 'closed' to the application's I/O processor, which settles every request it holds for the session (a tested example: a request queued behind a logout gets 401). Commits: 7a4b50a3.

entry.what: Bug (in core's ta_host_run, by the backtrace): a run whose actor-to-actor sends fill the event pool, or the slab (variables and strings), crashes the process with SIGSEGV instead of growing the segment between runs or reporting TA_RUN_EXHAUSTED. I spawned many user actors whose first event makes each send one event to one named room actor, on the default config, and expected the host to grow its pools as capacity.md says ('When a pool fills, the host grows that segment between runs'); the process died with no error. The smallest case: 200 actors of <state id="s"><onentry><send event="hello" target="tinyactors://x/@sink"/></onentry></state> and one named sink, then await host.idle(): exit 139 on node and bun, native and quickjs; 128 actors pass. system.maxEvents 1000 makes it pass; with maxEvents 100000, 1000 users sending 2 joins each still crash with maxActors 2000 (slab derived from it) and pass with instanceBytes 50 MB or stringBytes 10 MB, so the slab's growth in a run crashes too. Events sent by the application (host.send, 20,000 to one actor) do not crash. Workaround: chat.mjs sizes maxEvents (8 per actor), instanceBytes (4096 per actor) and stringBytes (512 per actor) for the whole population, so the host never grows in a run. For p4-surprises: a request to core.
entry.evidence: gdb on node 22.23.3: SIGSEGV in ta_host_run () from build/tinyactors.node, called from ta_napi_turn and ta_napi_loop_turn; bun 1.4.1 crashes too (a bun.report link). Repro: a host on the default config with charts sink (<state id="s"/>) and src (the onentry send above), host.spawnChart('sink', {name: 'sink'}), 200 x host.spawnChart('src'), await host.idle(). docs/guide/capacity.md, 'The sizes'
entry.resolution: Fixed in core (111ab9fe): drain() routed an effect that lives in the segment block while host_send_to grew that same segment and freed the block (heap use after free under ASan). The segment being drained now grows after its drain, then drains again; a done.invoke that found no room, dropped before, is made before the session ends and retried after growth. Tests: tinyactors-core/tests/unit/test_host_growth.c (each path) and tinyactors-napi/test/growth.test.mjs (the repro: 200 and 2000 senders, a foreach of 1000, 300 invokes). The chat-rooms workaround (sizing maxEvents, instanceBytes, stringBytes) is no longer needed. Commits: 4534196a (the test).

entry.what: Surprise: host.wake(session, blob) accepts an older blob of the same session and silently puts the actor back in that older state. I hibernated an actor (blob 1), woke it, sent it an event, hibernated it again (blob 2), and called wake with blob 1, expecting TA_ERROR_INVALID, since the error says 'TA_ERROR_INVALID: not its blob'; the wake succeeded and the actor's count went back from 2 to 1. A store that returns a stale copy (a failed overwrite that left the old file, a replica behind, a cache) loses state with no error, and nothing in hibernation.md says the application must make sure the blob is the latest. The example's store keeps the newest blob in memory until its file is written and chains each session's writes, so it never hands back an old one.
entry.evidence: spike, node 22.23.3: hibernate, wake(b1), send inc, b2 = hibernate, wake(b1) -> no throw, log '1 1' after the next inc; the error text from wake(a, otherSessionsBlob): 'the wake was refused (TA_ERROR_STATE: the session is not hibernated; TA_ERROR_INVALID: not its blob)'; docs/guide/hibernation.md, 'What a blob holds'
entry.resolution: Fixed in core: a hibernation notes the low 32 bits of the instance macrostep in the actor links (ta_actor_links, beside the actor pool), and ta_host_wake refuses a blob holding another macrostep with TA_ERROR_STALE (the actor stays hibernated); another session blob stays TA_ERROR_INVALID. A blob of the same macrostep holds the same state, since nothing changes it outside a macrostep. Cost: 4 B per actor slot of maxActors (links 12 to 16 B), a store at hibernation and a compare at wake, nothing per event. Tests: tinyactors-core test_host.c test_wake_refuses_an_older_blob; napi test/hibernation.test.mjs and cpython tests/test_hibernation.py. Commits: dcbe4f09, 9dc211ca (a newer blob after a restore; snapshots version 9).

On quickjs the same data is the application's realm. The README's Values section says a value is copied when it crosses, which made me expect plain objects of my realm; nothing says a handler gets the chart's realm. entry.resolution: Fixed in napi: what the native datamodel hands the application (send.data, so send.message.data, invocation.data) is the payload's value copied with the application's realm's constructors on its first read: the realm's script also runs in the application's own realm (runInThisContext, once per environment), and its kit's exported() copies arrays, plain objects and Uint8Arrays, an XML node as its text. instanceof Array holds and deepStrictEqual against a literal passes. Measured (scratchpad p4-surprises/bench-send.mjs: one actor sending {n, items: [1, 2, 3], name} by <content expr> to an I/O processor whose handler reads send.data.items, 20,000 sends a round, the least of 12 rounds, pinned to one CPU, builds alternating; x86_64 Linux, Intel Xeon @ 2.10GHz, 4 CPUs, another agent's builds running beside): node 22.23.3 11.37 / 11.57 / 11.74 us a send before, 12.49 / 12.67 / 12.69 after (about +1.0 us, 8 to 10 %); bun 1.4.1 7.35 / 7.80 before, 8.13 / 8.21 after (+0.4 to 0.8 us); with a handler that does not read data 10.58 before, 10.37 after on node: nothing. Test: test/effects.test.mjs 'send.data is the application\'s: its arrays are Arrays here, and XML content is its text'. Commits: 22a7eaf2.

entry.what: Docs gap: host.hibernate(session) on an actor that is already hibernated, or whose wake the host has asked for and not yet got, throws TA_ERROR_STATE, the same status as for an actor that is not at rest; index.d.ts and hibernation.md list only events waiting, in a step, or running an invocation. Only the message tells them apart ('... an invoked child), or not resident'). An eviction loop that keeps its own resident set (as the docs' pattern does) cannot tell 'try again later' from 'it is not here', so it must track residency itself, as chat.mjs does.

entry.resolution: Documented: docs/guide/hibernation.md, "When an actor cannot hibernate", lists every case of TA_ERROR_STATE (events waiting, a step not over, running an invoked child or service, not resident: hibernated or its wake asked for and not given), says the status cannot tell the passing cases from the last, and that an eviction loop knows its resident set itself; TA_ERROR_STALE for an ended or unknown session. index.d.ts's hibernate says the same. Each case checked by a spike on both datamodels. Commits: 7a4b50a3.

entry.resolution: Documented: the README ("Charts") says the prefix match takes join.refused for join and that two such actors answer each other for ever, and docs/guide/inspection.md, "Two actors that never rest", shows how to notice it with hostStats: between two readings with no input given, the loop's charts gain macrosteps and fuel and host.runnable stays above zero (a tested example: a watchdog names the busy charts, a terminate ends the loop); the fix is to name the answer so it does not extend the request. entry.what: Bug: the requests pool never grows, and an <invoke> of a service past it is error.execution, while capacity.md says 'When a pool fills, the host grows that segment between runs' and services.md says 'a segment grows the pool when it runs out'. I ran 2,000 subscriptions on the default config, each renewal an <invoke type="urn:billing:payments">; I expected the host to grow the pool as it grows the others. Instead the 17th invocation running at once (maxRequests' default is 16) raised error.execution in its actor, the chart (which handles no error.execution in charging) sat in charging for ever with invocations 0 and was never charged, and those actors could not migrate either (it showed up as 29 actors left on release 1 after three retry passes). The pool's capacity stays 16 whether the invocations start in one run or one per turn. In core, invoke() in src/system/route.c raises error.execution and returns TA_POOL_NONE when ta_system_request_alloc gives TA_NIL, so the host is never asked to grow (host.c has a TA_POOL_REQUESTS growth case that this path never reaches). For p4-surprises: a request to core (return TA_POOL_REQUESTS and park, as the other pools do), or the docs say maxRequests is a limit. Workaround: billing.mjs sizes system.maxRequests for every charge that may run at once.
entry.evidence: spike, node 22.23.3 and bun 1.4.1, native and quickjs: 40 actors of <state id="busy"><invoke type="urn:svc" src="x:y"/></state>, spawned one per turn on the default config: 16 started, 24 error.execution, hostStats pools[0].requests {capacity:16, used:16, highWater:16}; with system.maxRequests 64 all 40 start. 200 started in one run: 16 started, 184 error.execution. tinyactors-core/src/system/route.c, invoke(), the external branch; docs/guide/capacity.md, 'The sizes'; docs/guide/services.md, 'An invocation uses one of the host's requests'
entry.resolution: Fixed in core: an invoke that finds the requests pool full is started again by its step once the pool grew (ta_core_invoke_retry), and the run reports TA_RUN_EXHAUSTED with TA_POOL_REQUESTS, which the host grows as the other pools; maxRequests is where the pool starts. Test: tinyactors-core tests/unit/test_host_growth.c, test_external_invokes_fill_the_requests (240 invocations, none failed). The example keeps its maxRequests sizing until the binding batch removes the workarounds. Commits: d907f4c2.

entry.what: Missing API: migrationDone gives how many actors failed to move but not which, nor why. I migrated a population where some actors hold a Date (the native datamodel cannot write one out) and wanted, as an operator, the list of actors left on release 1 and the reason, to decide whether to fix the chart or wait. The result is { migration, migrated, failed, pending }, pending naming only what the timeout left; the failed ones are named nowhere, and the reason (which host.hibernate's error gives: "variable 'couponAppliedAt' cannot be stored ...") is not reported by the migration at all. To find them the example lists every live actor (actorList) and asks actorGet for each one's segment: one typed method per actor of the host, for a question about a few. Workaround: leftBehind() in examples/subscription-billing/rollout.mjs; the reason is found by calling host.hibernate on one of them.

entry.resolution: Fixed in core: ta_host_migration_failed reads the sessions a migration could not move, each a ta_host_migration_failure of the session and the status that refused it (TA_ERROR_UNSUPPORTED for a state that cannot be written out), as ta_host_migration_pending reads the pending ones (valid until the next run). Decided shape, both bindings: migrationDone/migration_done result.failed is a list of {session, reason}, reason the status by name, in place of the count (callers read its length). The datamodel message (which variable) is not carried: hibernate of the actor gives it. Tests: tinyactors-core test_host.c test_migration_names_the_failed; napi test/migration.test.mjs, cpython tests/test_migration.py. The example keeps its count (billing.mjs reads failed.length) and leftBehind() until the binding batch removes the workarounds. Commits: 43deb011.

entry.what: Docs gap: a state a migration enters is entered without its <onentry>. Version 2 made version 1's pastDue a compound state whose initial child, grace, armed the grace timer in its onentry; a version 1 actor in pastDue moved to pastDue.grace, as migration.md's 'its active states (matched by id)' led me to expect, but no grace timer was armed, so it would have stayed in grace for ever. A state version 2 does not have at all lands the actor in its parent's initial state, again with no onentry and no word in the upgrade event. architecture.md (ta_blob_migrate) says the configuration is 'completed top-down to a legal configuration' and that only invokes are started for the states the translation enters; the user's guide says neither. Workaround: the upgrade transition of subscription-v2.scxml arms the grace timer itself when In('pastDue').

entry.resolution: Documented: docs/guide/migration.md, "States the new version enters", says a migration enters states without their <onentry> (and leaves the old without <onexit>), that a state that became compound is entered at its initial child, that a state the new version does not have is replaced by its parent's initial state, and that the upgrade transition does the onentry's work with In(); a tested example on a SimulatedClock (pastDue becomes pastDue.grace with no onentry, paused lands in active, the upgrade transition arms the grace timer). Commits: 7a4b50a3.

entry.what: Behaviour that differs from the docs: a snapshot of an idle host on the runtime's clock holds the time of the host's last turn, not the time snapshot() was called, so after a restore every pending timer has back the time the host spent idle before the snapshot. snapshots.md says 'the host's clock goes on from the snapshot's time' and index.d.ts that the snapshot holds 'the host's time'; I expected that time to be when I called snapshot(), as a reader of a clock would, so that a turn timer with 6 s left at the snapshot has 6 s left after the restore. I spawned an actor with a delayed send of 1000 ms on a host without a SimulatedClock, waited 600 ms with the host idle, took host.snapshot() and restored it at once on the runtime's clock: the send came 1002 ms after the restore (nextDeadline 998.9), not 400 ms. With `await host.hostStatsAsync()` just before snapshot() (a typed method advances the host's clock at its post, and its reply's turn again) it came 400 ms after (nextDeadline 398.6); the same under bun (1004 ms and 400 ms). snapshot() does not advance the clock (src/host.c ta_napi_host_snapshot calls no ta_napi_advance; src/loop.c ta_napi_advance is called by inputs that depend on the clock, the turn, migrate and the typed methods). On a SimulatedClock the two agree, so testing.md's way of testing hides it. For p4-surprises: snapshot() advances the clock before it packs (as spawn does), or snapshots.md says the time is the last turn's. Workaround: examples/turn-game/game.mjs awaits host.hostStatsAsync() before each snapshot().

entry.resolution: Fixed in napi: snapshot() advances the host's clocks (ta_napi_advance) after its quiescence check and before it packs, so the snapshot holds the time of the call. Test: test/snapshot.test.mjs 'a snapshot holds the time of its call, and host.now() reads that clock on both hosts' (a 300 ms timer, 150 ms idle on the runtime's clock, restored with under 200 ms left). Commits: 827b4d29.

entry.what: A missing API: the host's clock cannot be read. To replay the inputs journaled after a snapshot, at the times they came, I need the host's time at the snapshot and at each input, on the runtime's clock. I expected a `host.now` (the host's clock in milliseconds, as SimulatedClock.now is a simulated one's), or the snapshot's time from snapshot() or hostStats; there is none: index.d.ts has only `nextDeadline` (relative to the last idle turn), hostStats has no time (requests.md, host.stats), and the snapshot's time is the last turn's (l-p4-examples-game-snapshot-time). So the example times its journal with performance.now(), relative to its own reading of it near the snapshot. Read after a typed method's reply (hostStatsAsync, then snapshot()), that reading was later than the host's time at the snapshot by the rest of the turn and the packing. On a loaded machine (4 CPU-bound loops and 4 test processes on 4 CPUs) that was enough, once in 8 runs, for a move that came within a few milliseconds of its turn's timeout to be replayed before the timeout although the host had judged it after: the spectators saw frame 5 of a match rewound (a timeout, then a move). For p4-surprises: a `host.now` read of the host's clock (ticks converted to ms), or the snapshot's time readable from the snapshot. Workaround: examples/turn-game takes its reading in the direct hostStats' onResult, which the drain calls just before the turn advances the host's clock (inferred from src/loop.c: drain, then ta_napi_advance; not documented), and 15 runs under the same load then rewound nothing; it replays each input after every deadline due by its journaled time, and its test allows a rewind only where a turn ended by a timeout in one history and by a move in the other.

entry.resolution: Built in napi: host.now(), the host's clock in milliseconds as it reads now (a SimulatedClock's time or ta_runtime_now_ns, with a restored host's offset), advancing nothing. Chosen over the time as last advanced because that one lags by however long the host was idle, the very error of game-snapshot-time: a journal records when each input came, which is now, on the clock the snapshot's time is on, so a replay on a restored host moves its SimulatedClock by entry.at - host.now(). Test: test/snapshot.test.mjs (the same case): now() before and after snapshot() brackets the restored host's now(), and moves with a SimulatedClock. Commits: 827b4d29.

entry.what: Behaviour that differs from the docs: maxOps bounds the engine's interrupt checks, not time, and a check costs far more than the quickjs guide implies. docs/guide/quickjs.md says the values of its example (maxOps 10_000) stop a while (true) {} and an allocating loop 'within milliseconds'; with maxOps 10_000, while (true) {} held the host 260 ms, and while (_event.data.value !== null) {} 2.5 s. The time per check depends on the code in the loop: 26 us for an empty loop, 250 us for one that reads a property, so the engine's default of 1,000,000 holds the host (and every host of the thread) 26 s for while (true) {} and 256 s (measured once) for the second loop. An operator choosing maxOps needs that number per check, and the guide's 'within milliseconds' is wrong by two orders of magnitude for its own example. Workaround: the example measures and configures maxOps 200 (5 to 50 ms) and states the measurements in its README.
entry.evidence: examples/iot-rules/measure.mjs holdTimes; node 22.23.3 on the Xeon of mise run measure: maxOps 1000: while (true) {} 26.9 ms, the guarded loop 246 ms; maxOps 200/2000/20000: 50/529/5074 ms; default: 25992 ms for while (true) {}, 255817 ms for the guarded loop; docs/guide/quickjs.md, 'The limits'
entry.resolution: Documented: docs/guide/quickjs.md, "The limits", says maxOps counts interrupt checks (one per 10,000 jumps and calls, JS_INTERRUPT_COUNTER_INIT), not time, with the measured hold times at 200, 1000, 10,000 and the default (while (true) {}: 6 ms, 27 to 39 ms, 260 ms, 26 s; a loop reading a property: 50 ms, 240 to 250 ms, 2.5 to 2.7 s, about 256 s; node 22 and bun 1.4.1 on the Xeon @ 2.10GHz, 2026-10-18), and recommends a few hundred for a service that answers requests and 1000 for background work, measured against the charts' real work; its example uses 1000, and the fuel and memory reasons of error.execution. Commits: 7a4b50a3.

entry.what: Missing API: compileCharts does not check a chart's JavaScript. An upload with cond="_event.data.value > limit)" or a <script> that does not parse compiles without a diagnostic; the syntax error is an error.execution at the expression's first evaluation, with no message and no line, on both datamodels. For a platform that takes charts from customers, the compile call is where a mistake should be reported, with its line, as it is for the XML (the README: 'A mistake in the XML, an unknown state id or a malformed attribute throws a CompileError here, before anything runs'). Workaround: examples/iot-rules/check.mjs finds every expression attribute and script with a regular expression and parses each with new Function (V8's or JavaScriptCore's parser, not QuickJS's), reporting file:line:column as the compiler does.
entry.evidence: examples/iot-rules/uploads/typo.scxml compiles; spike: cond="_event.data.v >" gave compiled with [] diagnostics and 'err error.execution undefined' at the first event, on native and quickjs
entry.resolution: Built in napi: compileCharts and compileSystem parse every expression and script of each "ecmascript" chart in the image with the engine (new vm.Script, in the shapes the native datamodel evaluates them in: a strict function for a value or a location, sloppy global code or a block for a script; nothing runs), and report each SyntaxError as a diagnostic: 'cond: SyntaxError: <the engine's message>' at the expression's element's line and column (the image's), a multi-line script's own line within it. A warning by default; with the new third argument {warningsAsErrors: true} (core's TA_COMPILE_WERROR, which also makes core's own warnings errors) an error, and the compile throws CompileError. Measured (scratchpad p4-surprises/bench-compile.mjs: the 196 converted W3C ecmascript charts compiled one by one, the least of 7 rounds, pinned to one CPU, builds alternating, same machine as the send benchmark): node 5.5 / 6.2 / 7.3 ms before, 8.7 / 8.8 / 12.8 ms after (about +15 to +35 us a chart); bun 10.4 ms before, 14.5 ms after. It finds 12 syntax errors there, all intentional (tests 152, 156, 277, 309, 312, 344, 457, 487, 488, 528, 553, 554), none else. Test: test/compile.test.mjs 'compileCharts parses each expression and script: a syntax error is a warning at its line, an error with warningsAsErrors'. examples/iot-rules compiles uploads with warningsAsErrors and drops its own checker of uploads. Commits: e6956f4e.

entry.what: Missing API: an error.execution says nothing about its cause, anywhere the application can read. A customer's rule that ran past maxOps, one that ran out of memoryLimit, one that threw new Error('boom'), one that called require: each is error.execution with _event.data undefined, the chart's errorsExecution counter goes up by one, and telemetry's span carries an scxml.action_failed event whose only attribute is scxml.action.opcode (7 for each of them). The README's Errors section says to turn on telemetry to learn which action failed; it marks the action but not why. So the platform cannot tell its customer 'your rule ran too long' or 'your rule threw boom'. Workaround: the inbox reports the counter's delta ('error.execution, 1') and the README says why there is no more.
entry.evidence: spike with telemetry and traceSpansDecodeAsync on quickjs and native: 'scxml.microstep spin {name: scxml.action_failed, attributes: {scxml.action.opcode: 7}}', the same for throw and hog; for a failed cond the event has no attributes at all
entry.resolution: Fixed in core: an optional datamodel vtable entry failure (ta_datamodel_failure: TA_DATAMODEL_FAILURE_EXCEPTION, _FUEL, _MEMORY and the exception text) that core asks on the error path only; error.execution then carries _event.data {reason: exception | fuel | memory, message} (message at most 256 bytes), made with from_wire, also for a send that fails in its own expressions (with its sendid). quickjs: fuel past max_ops, memory for the engine out of memory, else String(e); the napi native datamodel the exception text; the python datamodel Type: text, MemoryError as memory. A failure the host decides (an unknown send type) has no data. Cost: a store per evaluation. Tests: test_datamodel_ecmascript.c test_error_execution_says_why; napi test/datamodel.test.mjs; cpython tests/test_datamodel.py. Commits: 6a5df83d, 35ad9d58.

entry.what: Surprise with a sandbox: an untrusted chart on quickjs can end the application's process. A chart that does <invoke type="urn:shell" src="..."> of a type with no service makes the host throw 'no service is registered for the invoke type' from its turn; with no idle() waiting, that is an uncaught exception, which ends a Node.js process (Bun printed it and went on). The services guide says a failure is 'reported after the turn, as any handler's', and the quickjs guide promises that a bad chart gets error.execution and 'goes on with its next event'; nothing says the sandboxed chart picks the application's failure. The application cannot prevent it: the services option is read when the host is made (a Proxy that answers every type is never asked), and a handler cannot decline an invocation without throwing. Workaround: the platform waits on idle() after every input it makes into a rule's host and suspends the rule on a rejection, and main.mjs handles uncaughtException for the turns of a rule's own timers.
entry.evidence: examples/iot-rules/uploads/invoker.scxml; spike, node 22.23.3: 'TinyactorsError: no service is registered for the invoke type "urn:shell" at process.processImmediate', exit 1; with services = new Proxy({}, {get: ...}) the same, the trap never called
entry.resolution: Fixed in napi and cpython: an INVOKE whose type has no handler gives the invoker error.communication (the entry kept as failed until the UNINVOKE) and throws or raises nothing, restored or not; a handler that throws is still reported after the turn. Tests: napi test/services.test.mjs 'no service for the type is a communication error for the invoker, and nothing is thrown'; cpython tests/test_services.py test_no_service_for_the_type_is_a_communication_error_and_nothing_is_raised. examples/iot-rules drops its uncaughtException handler and its idle() watch; its invoker upload is an error.communication now. Commits: eec95150.

entry.what: Surprise: a <script> in a transition that declares with let or const at its top level runs the first time and is error.execution every later time, on both datamodels and both runtimes: the script runs as global code in the actor's context, so its second run redeclares the name. <transition event="go"><script>let n = 1; n + 1</script></transition> gave 'ran, error.execution, error.execution' for three go events; with var, 'ran, ran, ran'. A JavaScript programmer reads a script in a transition like a function body, whose let is fresh at each call. docs/guide/charts.md, 'Scripts', says such a script gives each actor a context of its own and keeps it resident, not that it can run only once. It also makes a rule cost a context per device: 62 KB resident on quickjs and 196 KB on native, against 2.5 KB and 2.1 KB for the same rule without the declaration. Workaround: the example's charts declare nothing (spin.scxml's loop was let tries = 0; while (true) ...; its second spin failed in 0.1 ms on the redeclaration, not on maxOps).
entry.evidence: spike, node 22.23.3 and bun 1.4.1, native and quickjs: let 'ran, error.execution, error.execution', const the same, var 'ran, ran, ran'; examples/iot-rules/measure.mjs costPerDevice(..., {declaring: true})
entry.resolution: Fixed in the compiler and both ECMAScript datamodels (the layer: core tells a chart-level script from one in executable content, the datamodels run them): a chart-level <script> is TA_EXPRESSION_GLOBAL_SCRIPT (global code, as before), one in executable content TA_EXPRESSION_SCRIPT, which quickjs and the napi native datamodel run in a block, so its let, const and class are its own at each run and declare nothing for the chart (a rule with let stays in the shared realm); var and function stay the session. The python datamodel treats both kinds as scripts and was already re-runnable. Images compiled before must be compiled again. Tests: test_datamodel_ecmascript.c test_executable_scripts_run_again (both realms); napi test/datamodel.test.mjs; cpython tests/test_datamodel.py (python and quickjs). Commits: fa0f761b, 156f9802, 85944c58.

entry.what: Bug (in core, by the code): done.state.<parallel> is raised while a region is still being entered. A transition that targets two shallow history states at once (target="legalWasAt financeWasAt", one per region of the parallel review), where the first region's history holds its final state and the second's a state that is not final, ended the review: done.state.review came although finance was in financeReviewing. Expected, as SCXML's isInFinalState: the parallel is done only when every region is in a final state, so no done.state.review. The same happens when a deep history re-enters the parallel (resume). A minimal chart (parallel p of regions a and b, a's history a2 final, b's b2 not; out -> target='ah bh') logged 'DONE.P' with In('b2') true and In('b3') false, on both datamodels; with target 'bh' alone nothing wrong happens. tinyactors-core/src/core/core.c:824 parallel_in_final checks only the active leaves under p, and runs at SUBPHASE_ENTER_FINAL (core.c:1690-1695) after the first region's final state is entered and before the second region's states are: a region with no active leaf yet does not count against it.
entry.evidence: spike, node 22.23.3: { p: { a: 'a2', b: 'b2' } } with done.state.p delivered; tinyactors-core/src/core/core.c:824-839, :1690-1695
entry.resolution: Fixed in core: parallel_in_final checks every region reached through parallel states, as SCXML isInFinalState does (a compound region needs an active final child), so a region not entered yet counts against done.state of the parallel while a transition enters the regions one after another. Test: tinyactors-test scenario parallel-history (M1): one event taking one region to its final state and the other not, then a re-entry through both shallow history states at once (target="ah bh"), then through a deep history state; it failed before the fix and passes on every implementation. The example keeps its guard until the binding batch removes the workarounds. Commits: 5a294b9f.

entry.what: Surprise and docs gap: inline XML <content> in a <send> to an I/O processor gives the application different things on the two datamodels, and on quickjs nothing. <send type="urn:x"><content><metadata xmlns="" id="doc-1"><title>Budget & plan</title></metadata></content></send>: on native, send.data is an XMLNode (the datamodel's DOM, a class with getElementsByTagName, getAttribute, toString), which the README's value table says a value cannot be ('a class's instance is refused'); on quickjs, reading send.data throws TinyactorsError TA_ERROR_INVALID 'the send's data could not be read'. I expected the same value on both, or a documented one (the XML as text, say). The same XML sent from the chart to itself is a DOM on both datamodels (_event.data.getElementsByTagName works), and actorContext shows an XML <data> as the DOM's plain tree on native and null on quickjs. docs/guide/charts.md, 'XML data', and io-processors.md say nothing about XML reaching the application.
entry.evidence: spike, node 22.23.3 and bun 1.4.1: native 'object XMLNode ... Budget & plan doc-1'; quickjs 'data err TA_ERROR_INVALID the send's data could not be read'
entry.resolution: Native half fixed in napi: an XML node that leaves a chart for the application is its XML text, a string (send.data, invocation.data: the document's source, or a node written out), and as a neutral value (to_wire, so actorContext and JSON.stringify in a chart) too, through XMLNode.prototype.toJSON. Test: test/effects.test.mjs 'send.data is the application\'s: ...'. quickjs still refuses reading such a send's data: requested of core, l-p4-surprises-quickjs-xml. docs/guide/charts.md, 'XML data', says both. The quickjs half fixed in core (l-p4-surprises-quickjs-xml): both datamodels give the XML text. Commits: 22a7eaf2, 19e88128.

entry.what: Docs gap: actorContext reads null for a variable that is undefined (<data id="u"/>), on both datamodels, while the README says undefined and null stay apart; and asked right after spawn, before the actor's first turn, it reads null for every variable, spawn params included (an actorState awaited first, which lets a turn run, shows them). inspection.md says such an actor's 'variables not yet set', not that they read null, so an admin view shows a new document with docID null, the same as a variable that holds null. requests.md says only 'A variable the datamodel cannot read or write as a neutral value is undefined or null'.

entry.resolution: Not the binding's decoding but core's encoding: actor.context wrote each variable with to_wire, whose ECMAScript rule makes undefined at the top null, and before the first macrostep every variable is undefined. Fixed in core (l-p4-surprises-context-undefined), on every datamodel: a variable holding undefined reads undefined, apart from null; before the first turn every variable is undefined, the spawn params included (index.d.ts, actorContext; docs/guide/inspection.md). Commits: 867b6934.

entry.what: Missing API: an admin view cannot show when an actor's delayed sends are due, nor where its history states would return. A document escalated or in revising reads only 'escalated' or 'revising' from actorState; which states a resume or a resubmission re-enters is in the history states, and when each stage's SLA breaches is a pending delayed send, and no typed method (actor.get, actor.state, actor.context) lists either. host.nextDeadline is the host's next deadline, of any actor. I expected actorGet or actorState to give an actor's pending sends (sendid, event, due) and its recorded histories, which is what an operator asks first ('when will this one escalate?').
entry.evidence: tinyactors-core/docs/requests.md, actor.get and actor.state: no timers or history in the results; index.d.ts ActorGetResult
entry.resolution: Left for the maintainer (the coordinator's triage: an API for what SCXML does not expose is new semantics). Recommendation: a read-only typed method of core's control plane, actor.timers (or two fields of actor.get), listing an actor's pending delayed sends (sendid, event, due in the host's clock) and its history states' recordings; it costs nothing per event, only the call, and each binding adds one typed method. Until then a chart keeps in a variable what an admin needs (the example keeps pausedStage), and the example's README says what an admin cannot see.

entry.what: Docs gap: an input given just before clock.increment(ms) is handled at the new time, not the time it was given, and host.nextDeadline read right after the input is still the last idle turn's. My test called shop.add('ann', 'tea', 3) (a reserve to the warehouse, whose hold is a 60 s delayed send) and then advanced the SimulatedClock 59 s deadline by deadline, expecting the hold made at 0 and due at 60 s. nextDeadline read undefined on both hosts (the input's turn had not run), so the loop made one increment(59000), the reserve ran at 59 s, and the hold came due at 119 s: the expiry case failed. testing.md always awaits idle() after an input, but neither it nor the README says that an input's actor runs at the next turn's clock, so an input and an increment in one tick reach the actor after the clock moved. Workaround: advance() settles both hosts before it reads nextDeadline.
entry.evidence: examples/inventory-sync/test.mjs, advance() (the settle at its start); without it a DEBUG print read 'advance 0 [] 59000' then 'advance 59000 [ 60000, 5000 ] 61000'; docs/guide/testing.md, 'Stepping the clock'
entry.resolution: Documented: docs/guide/testing.md, "Stepping the clock", says an input runs at the next turn's time and that nextDeadline still reads the last idle turn's, with a tested example (a reserve given before increment(59000) runs at 59000; await idle() between them when the input belongs first); the README's SimulatedClock section says it too, and index.d.ts's nextDeadline. entry.what: Docs gap in the pattern to copy: remote-python's transport (examples/remote-python/remote.mjs) and the other-systems guide write each send.message as a small frame on a TCP socket without socket.setNoDelay(true). A request whose answer is a frame (reserve, then reserved; a duplicated confirm, then message.fail) then waits for the peer's delayed ACK, about 40 ms on Linux loopback, because Nagle's algorithm holds the second small write. I expected a frame to arrive within a few event-loop turns on loopback: a settle loop of 2000 setImmediate turns ended with warehouse.link.received 5 against 6 frames the storefront had written, and the frame arrived only when I waited 300 ms. Not the package's behaviour but the transport's, which the package leaves to the application; the guide's 'Other systems' could say it. Workaround: Link.attach sets setNoDelay(true).
entry.evidence: examples/inventory-sync/link.mjs, attach(); the failing run: 'the systems never settled: {"shop":[15,24,true],"warehouse":[24,13,true],...}' (node 22.23.3)
entry.resolution: Documented: docs/guide/other-systems.md, "Over a socket", has a tested TCP transport (length-prefixed CBOR frames, both hosts in one process, port 0) that calls setNoDelay(true) on both ends and says why (Nagle's algorithm holds a small second write for the peer's delayed acknowledgement, about 40 ms on Linux loopback; asyncio sets TCP_NODELAY itself); examples/remote-python/remote.mjs sets it too. Commits: 7a4b50a3.

The warehouse's inventory() reads each SKU's name from its variables instead of matching sessions.

entry.resolution: Documented, the shape kept (the coordinator's triage): the README ("Actors, sessions and addresses") has a tested example of the comparison idiom (sessions.includes(Number(session)), sessions.map(BigInt).includes(session), a Map keyed by String(session)) and says includes(session) is false; docs/guide/inspection.md says it in bold where the typed methods' sessions are described. entry.what: Docs gap: a generated sendid is unique in its session only. Every session's first <send idlocation> gets 'send.1', on both datamodels, so two jobs' attempts arrive at an I/O processor with the same send.sendid. I kept the running workers in a Map keyed by send.sendid, as io-processors.md's table ('<send id>, or the id the host generated') and index.d.ts:319 suggest is enough, to abort them by the id the chart sends back; I expected a generated id to name the send in the host. What happened: one job's finished attempt deleted another's entry, and at a shutdown the hanging job's worker was missing from the scheduler's in-flight list (inFlight [] with job 'stuck' running). SCXML asks a generated id to be unique in the session, so this is correct; the docs could say 'unique in the sender's session: key by session and sendid'. Workaround: scheduler.mjs keys by `${send.session}:${send.sendid}`.
entry.evidence: a probe with two sessions of a chart whose onentry has <send type="urn:x" idlocation="sid"/>: 'native session 1n sendid send.1', 'native session 2n sendid send.1', the same on quickjs (node 22.22, 2026-10-18); docs/guide/io-processors.md:70, index.d.ts:319
entry.resolution: Documented: docs/guide/io-processors.md's table of a send's fields and index.d.ts's Send.sendid say a generated id is unique in the sender's session only (each session's first is send.1) and to key by session and sendid; docs/guide/charts.md's <send> table says it for idlocation. Commits: 7a4b50a3.

entry.what: Awkward shape: host.idle() on a closed host throws TA_ERROR_STATE ('the Host is closed') at the call instead of returning a rejected promise. I wrote `await assert.rejects(host.idle(), ...)` after close(), as index.d.ts:988-993 says idle() 'Rejects ... with TA_ERROR_STATE when the host is closed first'; I expected a promise-returning method to reject, since a caller writes `host.idle().catch(...)` or `await` without a try around the call. What happened: the throw escaped assert.rejects's promise argument. An idle() already waiting when close() runs does reject, so the two cases differ. Workaround: the test asserts the throw (assert.throws) and the rejection of an idle() taken before close() separately.
entry.evidence: node and bun: `host.close(); try { host.idle() } catch (e) { ... }` prints 'threw synchronously TA_ERROR_STATE the Host is closed'; examples/job-scheduler/test.mjs, the idle() test
entry.resolution: Fixed in napi: idle() on a closed host returns a promise rejected with TA_ERROR_STATE ('the Host is closed') instead of throwing at the call; idle() on another object still throws its TypeError. Test: test/loop.test.mjs 'idle() on a closed host returns a rejected promise'; examples/job-scheduler asserts the rejection. Commits: 827b4d29.

entry.what: Docs gap: nothing says that an open host with no pending deadline keeps nothing alive, so the process exits with the host open and actors still waiting. README.md:247, :501 and index.d.ts:905 say an open host with a pending deadline keeps the process alive; the converse is left to inference. I expected to have to close the host for the process to exit (a JavaScript programmer expects an open handle object to hold the loop, like a server or a socket). What happened, and what this example relies on: a batch whose last job ended exits by itself with host.closed false (beforeExit fires, nextDeadline undefined); and a job waiting for an async I/O processor whose promise has no I/O behind it (a worker that hangs on `new Promise(() => {})`) lets the process exit with the job unfinished, unless the chart armed a timeout. The README's 'Before you use it' could say both: the host's one timer is the only thing it keeps alive, and an actor waiting for an answer is not.

entry.what: Missing API: a chart cannot read the host's time, so a recurring job that keeps its cadence needs a round trip through an I/O processor for every tick. I wrote a recurring job as SCXML's usual chained <send event="due" delay="20ms"/> armed at each tick; each delay counts from the step that armed it, which runs late by the timer's and the turn's latency, so the job falls behind every tick: 24 ms behind after 40 ticks of 20 ms alone, 136 ms beside a CPU-bound job (main.mjs --drift). I expected a way to arm a send at an absolute time, or to read the host's clock in an expression (as the application cannot either: l-p4-examples-game-host-clock). Date.now() in a native chart is the wall clock, not the host's, and wrong on a SimulatedClock. Workaround: the chart keeps its schedule as absolute times of the application's clock (start, nextDue, given at spawn) and asks the urn:jobs:clock processor for the time before arming each tick (delayexpr nextDue - now); the job is then late by one tick's latency only (1.2 ms alone, 7.3 ms under load). The docs could at least say that a chained delayed send drifts by its latency on the real clock.
entry.evidence: examples/job-scheduler/charts/job.scxml (the clock transition); main.mjs --drift output in examples/job-scheduler/README.md, 'Drift' (node 22, x86_64 Linux, 2026-10-18)
entry.resolution: Left for the maintainer (the coordinator's triage: a clock a chart can read is outside SCXML). Recommendation: keep SCXML's relative delays, and if the maintainer wants a clock in charts, offer it as a platform system variable under _x (SCXML reserves _x for the platform), such as _x.now(), the host's clock in milliseconds, which a SimulatedClock moves too; core would give the datamodels a read of the host's time, nothing per event. Meanwhile the README ("Time and the SimulatedClock") says a chained delayed send drifts by its latency on the runtime's clock and gives the pattern examples/job-scheduler uses (absolute times from the program, the time asked of an I/O processor before each delay). Commits: 7a4b50a3.
